payload.title: Italian Marriage Recognition in Australia Explained
payload.primary_keyword: is marriage in italy recognised in australia
payload.audience: Australian couples in their 30s, affluent, interested in a destination wedding in Italy and later luxury celebrations; about AUD 150k budget for the destination wedding
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s, about AUD 150k set aside for an Italian wedding and planning a second celebration (or more) back home, who want a straight answer to 'will our Italian wedding count in Australia?' before they commit: whether it is legally valid here, what they must do (and need not do) once home, which document proves it to which agency, how a surname change works in their state, and whether it is smarter to marry legally in Australia and keep Italy symbolic.
payload.goal: Speak with a Wedded Advisor to decide between a legal Italian ceremony and a legal-at-home plus symbolic-in-Italy plan, and to have the paperwork handled (Wedded Concierge consultation).
payload.angle: Page-one answers stop at 'yes, overseas marriages are generally recognised'. This post answers the next five questions an Australian couple actually has: the exact test in Part VA of the Marriage Act 1961 and the exceptions that can break it; why there is no registration step in Australia and what that means in practice; how you prove the marriage afterwards (Italian certificate, multilingual extract, apostille, NAATI translation) and which Australian agencies are known to accept what; why NSW and Victoria make a surname change a separate application; and what a symbolic Italian ceremony or a later Australian celebration does and does not do legally, including the position for same-sex couples, where Italy offers a civil union rather than marriage. Italy and Australia specific throughout, with the step-by-step for marrying in Italy left to the sister guide.
must_include: Direct answer in the first 60 words: in most cases yes, if the marriage is valid under Italian law and would have been valid under Australian law, citing Smartraveller and the Attorney-General's Department (re-check fact_38, fact_39)

The legal test: Marriage Act 1961 Part VA, s 88D, plus the s 88D(2) exceptions in plain English (already married, under age where domiciled in Australia, prohibited relationship, no real consent) [[VERIFY: s 88D wording against the current compilation on legislation.gov.au]]

No registration in Australia: you cannot register an Italian marriage or get an Australian marriage certificate, and the marriage should be registered in Italy at the comune; what to keep instead (re-check fact_41, fact_42)

Proving it at home: the Italian marriage certificate or atto, the multilingual extract (estratto plurilingue, Vienna Convention 1976, not issued for civil unions), the Prefettura apostille, and NAATI translation where a full Italian-language document is used; a short table of which proof suits which use (passport, Medicare, banks, Services Australia, visas) with any agency claim sourced or marked [[VERIFY: Australian Passport Office and Services Australia requirements for overseas marriage certificates and translations]]

Changing your surname by state: NSW and Victoria require a change of name application because an overseas certificate cannot be used directly; other states and territories stated only if sourced, otherwise [[VERIFY: QLD, WA, SA, TAS, ACT, NT rules for using an overseas marriage certificate to change surname]]; note that this is a name-change rule, not a recognition problem

Legal at home first, symbolic in Italy: how it works (Notice of Intended Marriage at least 1 month ahead, re-check fact_37), what a symbolic Italian ceremony is legally (no legal effect), and the trade-offs for couples who want the Italian day to be 'the' wedding

Later celebrations: a second ceremony, reception or vow renewal in Australia after a legal Italian wedding has no legal effect and you cannot marry each other again if Australia already recognises the marriage (re-check fact_43); what to tell a celebrant

Same-sex couples: Italy offers the unione civile (Law 76/2016), not marriage; Australia recognises same-sex marriages performed overseas since 9 December 2017; the Australian status of an Italian civil union stays [[VERIFY: how Australia treats an Italian unione civile]] unless an official source is found; marrying legally in Australia first as the clear option
avoid: Repeating the sister guide's Atto Notorio, Nulla Osta, Prefettura and comune steps or its timeline; one sentence and a link to /destination-weddings/getting-married-in-italy

Repeating the general all-countries pages; Italy and Australia specific only, with links to /expert-advice/do-you-have-to-register-an-overseas-marriage-at-home, /expert-advice/overseas-marriage-certificate and /expert-advice/should-you-marry-legally-abroad-or-have-a-symbolic-ceremony
Any fee figure: write 'a fee applies'
Legal advice framing: describe the rules, note they change, and point to Smartraveller, the Attorney-General's Department, state registries and a lawyer for individual circumstances
Saying an Italian civil union is recognised as a marriage in Australia, or any recognition claim without an Australian government source
Business details not yet confirmed: Concierge fee model, deposits, From AUD ranges, Wedded Privileges detail, a named Advisor, real weddings
Competitor wording, claims or images (including Easy Weddings)
Stacked superlatives, exclamation marks, em dashes, US spelling
